title: Migration safety & cost-guarantee battlecard
content:
TL;DR: This battlecard is a playbook to help sellers and solutions engineers position Redwood for customers evaluating migration from other LLM API vendors. Focus: reduce migration risk (latency/cost/regression), guarantee predictable unit economics via SLO-driven runbooks, and win on observable rollback/canary controls. Offer concrete rebuttals to the common traps (model parity, hidden per-token costs, tail-latency, tokenization mismatch).

KEY VALUE PROPS (short scripts)
- For product leaders: "We make migration predictable: you get a migration plan with canary SLOs, cost parity tracker, and a rollback policy—so you can swap endpoints without surprise bills or outages."
- For infra/platform teams: "We give you traffic shaping, model pinning, and traceable cost attribution per route so you can enforce budget controls and fast rollback."
- For engineering leads: "We reduce unit cost while preserving latency with automatic prefix caching, workload-aware batching, and quantization recommendations that are reversible."

CUSTOMER MIGRATION SCENARIOS (most common)
1) Burst-traffic SaaS: worried about tail latency during marketing spikes. They need predictable p95/p99 and a canary plan.
2) Regulated enterprise: requires private deployment & audit logs and wants to compare on-prem vs hosted risk.
3) Cost-migration: teams pay a lot on incumbent per-token pricing and want a plan to lower TCO without degrading QA metrics.
4) Model-lock fear: customers think the incumbent has proprietary model features (response style, instruction-following) and worry about parity.

FEATURE COMPARISON (how to frame vs typical LLM API providers)
- SLAs & SLO Workflows: Redwood = SLO-first migration templates (canary thresholds, automated rollback), Incumbent = limited or opaque rollback policies.
- Cost Visibility: Redwood = token + route level cost breakdown and forecasting, Incumbent = aggregated billing, hidden surges for long-context workloads.
- Observability: Redwood Console exposes token-level traces, KV-cache hit rates, and per-request kernel selection; Incumbent often has request logs only.
- Operational Controls: Redwood = per-route throttling, policy routing (latency vs cost), pin model versions; Incumbent = coarse throttling and slower model switching.
- Private / Dedicated parity: Redwood Private provides same control plane and tooling as hosted API; competitors often degrade features in private deployments.

COMMON TRAPS PROSPECTS RAISE, WITH REBUTTALS
1) Trap: "Your outputs won't match our current model's style or hallucination profile."
   Rebuttal: "We run side-by-side evals on your prompt corpus during the migration window, surface delta reports (precision/recall, hallucination rate), and provide a rollback to the incumbent endpoint while we tune a compatible model variant. We can run prompt transforms or small finetune/PEFT passes under a canary for parity."

2) Trap: "We can't risk increased latency/tail spikes during migration."
   Rebuttal: "Migration plan includes traffic shaping: start at 1% traffic, measure p50/p95/p99 and worker queuing metrics, then ramp using automated SLO gates. If tail exceeds threshold we automatically shift traffic back and log a postmortem."

3) Trap: "Your pricing looks cheaper on paper but hidden costs will appear (context windows, long sessions)."
   Rebuttal: "We run a cost-simulation on a week's production traffic sample (token-level replay) and deliver an itemized savings report with sensitivity to context length and cache hit rates — plus configuration suggestions (kv-cache, batching, quantization) that you can opt into."

4) Trap: "We rely on proprietary features (tool-calling, function-calling) only available in their stack."
   Rebuttal: "We support function-calling and structured output; if there are subtle behavior differences we’ll run compatibility tests and, if needed, extend a compatibility shim as part of the migration SOW."

TECHNICAL SELLING POINTS (SE talking points)
- Demo: live traffic-swap in a staging environment (show canary ramp and SLO gate trip).
- Show Redwood Console: token-level cost by route, KV-cache warmup graph, and per-token latency heatmap.
- Show rollback: simulate an injected regression and hit the rollback button; show time-to-rollback metric.

OBJECTION HANDLING SCRIPTS (short)
- Objection: "We can just keep using the incumbent, why move?"
  Reply: "If predictability and unit-cost are in scope, our migration reduces your monthly spend while preserving availability. We’ll prove it on your traffic sample and include an SLO-backed pilot."
- Objection: "We don’t want vendor lock on deployment features."
  Reply: "Redwood separates control plane and data plane and supports private deployments and cloud-provider neutralizable configs. You can take the runtime artifacts on-prem as needed."

SELLING PLAYS (step-by-step)
1) Pre-sell: Request a 7-day production traffic sample (tokenized). Run cost-sim and delta evals. Deliver the "Migration Quick Sheet" showing estimated savings and risk matrix.
2) Pilot: Launch 1% traffic canary for 48 hours with SLO gates. Daily sync with engineering.
3) Ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% with automated cost/latency alerts and a scheduled rollback window.
4) Optimize: Post-cutover, run Optimize toolkit recommendations (quantization candidate list, batching tweaks) and measure 90-day realized unit cost.

COMPETITIVE VULNERABILITIES TO EXPLOIT
- Opaque billing models: push token-level replay to show discrepancies.
- Weak canary tooling: emphasize our SLO automation and quick rollback capability.
- Private deployment feature gaps: highlight parity of console/rollout features in our Private offering.

PLAYBOOK ASSETS (what SEs should bring to meetings)
- "Migration Quick Sheet" (1-pager): baseline cost, expected savings, SLO gates, timeline.
- Sample postman/curl snippet for traffic swap.
- Demo script for 10-minute live canary.
- Eval report template: side-by-side response diffs and hallucination metrics.

TEMPLATE CUSTOMER EMAIL (to book pilot)
Subject: Quick pilot to validate cost and latency for model endpoints

Hi <Name>,

We can validate migration risk in 2 steps: 1) a 7-day tokenized replay to produce an itemized cost and compatibility report, and 2) a 48-hour 1% traffic canary with SLO gates. If this sounds good I’ll loop in engineering and send the data-sharing instructions.

Best,
Aisha (solutions@redwood.ai)

NEXT ACTIONS / TODOs
- [ ] Build "Migration Quick Sheet" template (owner: Marcus) — JIRA: RED-7891
- [ ] Add canary demo to SE playbook deck (owner: Sofia) — due 2025-02-07
- [ ] Automated cost-simner endpoint for token replay (infra PR referenced above)

OPEN QUESTIONS (internal)
- What legal language can we offer for a cost-savings guarantee pilot (need legal review)? (Ping: Ben/Legal)
- Can private deployments include the same console SLA? profile of support needed?

NOTES TO SELF / OBSERVATIONS
- Prospect wins when we show a real tokenized replay with their data. SEs should push for that early.
- Avoid promising exact model parity; instead promise measurable parity checks and rollback.
- Scripts above assume SE has access to the customer's prompt corpus or a representative sample. If not, run synthetic behavioral tests tied to user journeys.
